title: Character Portraits
author: Kurt Wootton
summary: Wootton, drawing on thirty-five years studying literacy development, argues that reading instruction has gotten much more precise about decoding and fluency but has correspondingly neglected what happens when a reader stays with a text long enough to reach deep comprehension. He criticizes the common classroom habit of testing initial encounters with a text (the 'dreaded pop quiz' on last night's reading) rather than scaffolding students toward deeper understanding after that first pass. He illustrates his alternative with a professional-development session he led for North Star Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, built around Frida Kahlo portraiture and the picture book Frida and Her Animalitos, where an energetic 'Wild Reading' performance of the text was explicitly not treated as evidence of comprehension. The core technique he describes, 'Character Portraits,' has students return to the text in small groups to build an evidence-based 'word portrait' of a character using direct quotations, a four-step process (choose a character, return to the text, build a word portrait, share and discuss) he says works from early elementary through secondary novels, short stories, and plays.
points: Wootton argues literacy instruction has become precise about decoding and fluency but has neglected what happens when readers stay with a text long enough to reach deep comprehension.

He criticizes the common practice of assessing students' first encounter with a text (e.g., a pop quiz on last night's reading chapter) rather than scaffolding a return to the text for deeper meaning.
The 'Character Portraits' technique requires students to build an evidence-based word portrait of a character using direct textual quotations, not paraphrase or general impression.

He reports the activity, demonstrated with Frida and Her Animalitos in a K-5 professional development session, works equally well for secondary students reading longer novels, short stories, or plays.
quotes: But I wonder if, in becoming more precise about how reading works, we've paid less attention to what happens when a reader stays with a text—what happens when we really spend time with a book, wrestle with it, and work to reach a deeper understanding of it.

In the daily life of schooling, it's at this stage that I think we mistakenly build in assessments of student learning. Middle or high school students might be assigned a chapter of a book at night and then return to class to be greeted by the dreaded "pop quiz.
It was certainly wild and engaging, but as mentioned above, a lively reading doesn't necessarily show actual comprehension of the text.

I explained how important it is for students to return to the text to find evidence—hence the importance of using actual quotes from the text. What I loved seeing was how participants had the actual books in hand and were flipping pages, rereading passages, and discussing what the text revealed about Frida.
Reading a text once is just the beginning. After initially reading the text, students need to return to it, spend time with it, and discover meanings they may not have noticed on an initial reading.
